newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - One year on, Tradepoint says progressing.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - One year on, Tradepoint says progressing.

text.p: A year after launching as a rival to the London Stock Exchange (LSE), Tradepoint is planning the next moves in its battle to grab a share of the multi-billion pound business of trading equities in London.

Interviewed a year after it booked its first trade -- 100,000 shares in Hanson -- Tradepoint executive director Stephen Wilson told Reuters the firm planned to expand from British equities into continental European equities and even into bonds.
He said Tradepoint's British equity business had grown steadily in the past year and he pointed to the live buy and sell prices flicking across its trading screens as proof of its progress.
"There it is," he said, "and it works."
There is even an innovation since launch -- a colour-coded ticker-tape style panel showing stocks where Tradepoint's buy or sell prices are better than on the LSE's official Seaq screens.
But Wilson admitted the going remains tough as newcomer Tradepoint attempts to break the ingrained share trading habits of the London stock market.
"It is fair to say we have not reached critical mass," he told Reuters, "but one by one we are able to take each objection to using Tradepoint and show that in practice it works."

Wilson said Tradepoint is on course for its break-even target of capturing two percent of share trading in London by the end of 1997 -- but he conceeded it was still well short of that goal, even on its busiest days.

For Wilson the key point about Tradepoint's first year is that the share trading network has proved that it is capable of offering a viable alternative to the LSE, where shares can be traded in bulk and at keener prices than on the main exchange.
Now he says the system is well enough proven for the onus increasingly to be on performance-conscious fund managers to justify why they do not use it -- rather than why they do.
"We have seen quite a lot of fence sitters coming off the fence," he said, "saying you havn't gone away and it is getting to the point where we can't ignore you any more."

Originally conceived in Wilson's time at the LSE, Tradepoint's so-called order-driven approach involves buy and sell orders being matched by computer without the need for a middle man or market-maker.
Since last November, the LSE has been publicly committed to offering an order-driven alternative to its market-maker system, where traders quote prices on screen and agree trades by phone.
Yet the LSE is still locked in debate about detailed aspects of its reform and does not plan to introduce a quote-driven system until Spring 1997.

Anyway, Wilson believes Tradepoint's flexible and cost- conscious approach will continue to give it an edge even when the LSE's system is up and running. "Our position is to be the lowest cost exchange in the world," he said.
Wilson says Tradepoint has already increased its list of members to 64 from 42 at launch and says the company is targeting a further 100 customers -- mainly fund managers.
Wilson admitted the key to reaching its share trading target came down to its credibility in allowing members to trade.

"It all comes down at the end of the day to liquidity and what you do to get it," he said. "So far we don't have the critical mass for the snowball effect to start happening but we have lots of examples showing it definitaly has begun."
As he speaks, the Tradepoint screen shows 50,000 shares in mobile phone operator Orange being traded at within the price quoted on the LSE's Seaq screens.
"That is the excitement of this market," he said. "It is very real, the price on the screen is the price at which you can trade and that is such an important difference."
